It opens to the first endpoint that completes the handshake, implements the port's SessionEngine and SessionDrive over session-core's application layer (the observer keeps the subscribers, what the peer declared and the matching watches), and keeps its non-Send state behind one lock, handing samples and matching changes to C callbacks after the lock is released (D8), so a callback may re-enter its session as in zenoh-pico. The crate depends on `zenoh-collections` (its own `std` off, as upstream's) and, for `test`, on `rand`.

Memory safety does not rest on callers' promises: `unsafe_slice!` and `unsafe_slice_mut!` are checked indexing in every build (upstream's are unchecked outside tests), `vec::uninit` returns zeroed bytes (upstream sets a vector's length over memory it has not written, so every read of it is undefined), every `with_slot` panics on a reported count past the slot (upstream trusts it and sets a length past the bytes), and `ZBufWriter` holds the buffer by a mutable borrow and finds its slice at each write where upstream keeps a raw pointer to the buffer and a borrow into it at once. The one raw pointer left is a slice writer's mark, whose rewind now refuses a mark that is not of the slice the writer was cut from the front of; upstream takes any mark of the same lifetime.

Marks are checked where upstream's are not: `BBuf::rewind` refuses a length past its capacity, `ZBufReader::rewind` a position not in the buffer, `ZBufWriter::rewind` a byte past what its last slice holds (upstream panics or accepts each); `ZSlice::subslice` takes bounds at the largest number as a refusal and not an overflow; `AdvanceableReader::advance` takes the distance of the smallest `isize` as a distance and not an overflow.

Two faults of upstream's are not copied, each pinned on both sides by the differential test: `ZBufReader::read_u8` reports that there is nothing to read when the cursor stands at the end of a slice that has bytes after it, which `backtrack` (and so `seek` and `advance` backwards) leave it at whenever it lands on a slice boundary and which an empty slice is, where `read` goes on to the next slice (wz steps past it); and two buffers of the same bytes are unequal if one has an empty slice at its end (wz compares the bytes).

Round 3544.decision_summary: D3's first part lands: the locator directory, a zid's candidate locators held as soft state. Identity and location are separate, so a locator is a hint for reaching a zid, and since D4 a dial made from a hint closes at the InitAck if another node answers. The table is a fixed number of rows with no allocator, so every profile holds it. A row is a zid and a locator; each source (declared, Hello, link-state) confirms it with its own end, and a lookup never returns a hint whose every confirmation has ended. The lifetime is the source's to give, since only it knows its refresh period: the directory is the mechanism, the sources hold the policy. Declared hints are permanent and never evicted; a full table displaces the soft hint that ends first, and refuses, counted, when only declared hints are left. Candidates come declared first, then newest first. The round also repays the hosted C1cb count Round 3537 moved from 29 to 31.

Round 3550.decision_summary: D5's first part lands: each peer a node is told to hold gets a connection machine, written in SCXML and generated by SCE like the session machine. The model is BGP's peer machine: open is ManualStart, close is ManualStop, a failure or a lost session backs off on a retry timer, and a refusal is a state whose child names the cause (no locator, no slot, another node answered, the authority refused), held until the next open. A second open or close has no transition, so D6's idempotency is the machine's shape rather than a check. The host classifies every outcome and raises the event that names it, so no transition has a cond, and every effect is a duty the host performs after the event, which keeps the machine a pure function of its events. PeerTable holds one machine per zid with no allocator, reuses an Idle entry when full and refuses, counted, only when every entry holds a peer to keep. The duty record the multicast machines kept privately is shared now.

A session outlives its link: the link is up, being dialled, or waiting to be, and each step of the session moves it on, so a stepped program or its read task brings the link back without blocking a caller. On a completed handshake the session declares again its key expressions, subscribers and Interests under their ids, as pico resends its declaration cache; the entity tables are the record, so what is declared while the link is down is sent then. An open no endpoint answers still fails. The engine also gains the KeepAlive and Close codecs it lacked since step 3a.

Round 3572.decision_summary: Open-debt item 924, step 5: the last copy the unit-size sweep left (owner: do what is left). A WebSocket message that is one masked frame, which is every frame a client sends, was logged as an unmasked copy on both doors. The masking key is the last four bytes of the frame's header, so it stands in the stream just before the payload: the place is LogPlace::StreamMasked, the list keeps where the payload stands and unmasks it as it reads (a copy that lives for the read, not for the row), and the row's stream dependence reaches back over the key, so a byte ceiling that releases the key keeps the message whole first. A masked row on the lent door costs the same at 16, 256 and 4096 bytes (139.4 B), as an unmasked one does, and the handed door holds the stream's copy and no more. Only a message joined out of fragments stands nowhere in the stream and is still logged, which the redecode gate asserts is small and the only thing logged.

Round 3579.decision_summary: D6's first part: close and reset are the verbs D6 names. A close takes the peer out of the node's intent, then orders its sessions closed; the intent is a port of its own (PeerIntent), held apart from the sessions' directory, because a reset ends the sessions and keeps the intent. On AP the face loop's reconcile channel is that port: Withdraw stops every machine that held the node (manual.stop), its own and each configured endpoint's whose last session reached it, so the planner keeps the zid each peer's last session named. reset/<generation> is the one verb whose key carries an argument, and the grammar says so. Round 3600.decision_summary: The router's promise test (E7s, a router told 1.32% of a core that holds 1100 sessions) failed in four of the five hosted runs that finished from 16:18 UTC on 2026-10-24, with 148 to 501 clients lost, and passed on three fleet hosts. The router admits sessions at the emission cost it reads while the host is quiet (0.3 to 1.2 us) and holds them when it is loaded (6 to 19 us), so its keepalives fall later each second until the leases run out together; no bound at admission undoes that. A router that declared a share now reads the lateness of its keepalive timers once a second, on a thread of its own, and past an eighth of 2T/3 closes the newest sessions down to an eighth of what it holds, caps admission there, and recovers by doubling then adding (AdmissionControl, in the shape of TCP's reaction to a timeout). The keepalives of the sessions it closes stop before their closes are written.

Round 3608.decision_summary: Two policies bound what a blocking push costs when its link has no room. tx-no-progress-deadline adds a second bound beside the total wait: a window with no fragment of the message going out, in microseconds (TX_NO_PROGRESS_WINDOW_US), that a fragment out starts again without making the total longer, so the message is given up on at whichever bound comes first; off is upstream, the total wait alone. tx-expiry-keeps-session decides what the expiry costs: off is upstream, the session closes as unresponsive and the sender is told nothing; on drops the message, answers the sender TransportUnavailable and keeps the session. Both unicast push and the router egress sweep ask one decision point, SessionLinkActions::settle_blocking_expiry, so they cannot disagree. A droppable message and a probe are untouched.

Round 3615.decision_summary: The policy entity-timestamp-opt-in makes the timestamp something an entity takes part in only if it says so. Off is upstream: a subscriber and a querier see the timestamp of what they receive and a publisher attaches what it is given. On changes what a declaration that says nothing gets, and each declaration can state its own choice: SubscribeOptions and QueryOptions carry expose_timestamp, and a callback that does not expose it is handed a view that answers as a sample or reply with no timestamp and is the inner view in every other way. It is applied where a subscriber is registered and inside the consolidating sink of a query, so consolidation still orders by the stamp the callback is not shown. A publisher declared to stamp takes a time per message (put_at, delete_at) and supplies its own session's identity beside it, so a caller cannot sign as another node; one declared not to stamp refuses with StampedPutError::NotStamping and sends nothing.

Both read what a session reports of its peers, so the model left the tokio engine: wz_session_core::face holds FaceSnapshot, LinkSnapshot, GroupLink, FaceEventKind and the sink type, and builds a snapshot from a session's own SessionLinkActions; wz-capi-core re-exports them. Round 3623.decision_summary: Phase 1 of the router with a task per face (docs/router-task-per-face.md): the router's counts are atomics. RouterForwarder counted what it did with 21 Cell<usize>, which is right while one task drives every face and wrong when two do: a Cell is not Sync, and x.set(x.get() + 1) from two threads loses an increment. Each is now a Counter (router_forward/counter.rs), an AtomicUsize with Relaxed ordering: a counter publishes nothing and no decision on its value must agree with another memory location, so what it must keep is that no increment is lost, which every atomic read-modify-write does at any ordering. Round 3631.decision_summary: The fixed-memory slot node no longer repeats its whole declaration list after one refused send. Each session keeps a ReplayCursor in place of the declared flag, a tick runs one replay turn over the static declaration slice, and a send the session's stage refuses puts the cursor back on the entry that failed, so the entries that went out are not sent again. A node can now ask whether every established session has been told every declaration (declarations_synced). The session keeps declared() and mark_declared(), because the lwIP slot node sends its declarations in one step and has no sequence to resume. This is phase 4 of the pacing design for the slot node; the cooperative engine's redeclare stays with its owner.

Round 3634.decision_summary: The policy declaration-sync-pacing paces the declaration replay of a reconnect, on the heap runtime, the first host of ReplayCursor. Off is upstream and the default: one call sends every declaration. On sends them in turns of DECLARATION_SYNC_BURST_MESSAGES with DECLARATION_SYNC_INTERVAL_MS between, and the reconnect supervisor serves the session between turns in one task, so a failing turn ends the drive with its error. The cache and the cursor now live in one value, DeclarationCache, and every live declaration and retraction goes through a per-kind method of SessionLinkActions that records it and asks the cache what to do about the peer: a declaration made while a replay runs is owed and sent in its turn after what it depends on, and the retraction of one the peer was never told of sends nothing. A refused send resumes where it failed. The final-timeout limit of the design is not declared: no code reads it yet.

Round 3638.decision_summary: A session reports whether its declarations are synced, and a caller can wait for them to hold still. declarations_synced is true when no paced replay is owed and every interest the node sent that asks for what exists now (a liveliness subscriber with history, a liveliness get, a matching interest with current) has had the Declare(DeclFinal) that carries its id, or has waited DECLARATION_SYNC_FINAL_TIMEOUT_MS. The peer's own initial final is not required, since a router never sends one to a client. wait_declarations_stable(timeout) is true once the session is synced and the cache generation has not moved for one DECLARATION_SYNC_INTERVAL_MS, so a declaration made or withdrawn during the wait restarts it. The query is always on: the timeout limit is read whether or not declaration-sync-pacing is on. The bookkeeping is a pure value that reads no clock.

Round 3643.decision_summary: Phase 4 of declaration-sync pacing for the cooperative engine: its declarations take the replay cursor. Core::redeclare told six lists to a new link in one call and ignored every refused send. A per-link ReplayCursor (engine/replay.rs of wz-capi-coop) now walks the lists in a fixed order (key expressions, subscribers, Interests, queryables, tokens, liveliness subscribers), an entry's place being its kind's offset plus its index. A link that comes up begins the cursor and sends the first turn; poll_link sends later turns when due and the read's idle wait is shortened to the next one. Every live push into or removal from a list asks the cursor: a declaration it has not reached is sent in its turn, one behind it at once, a retraction is sent only if the peer was told of the entry. A lost or ended link discards the cursor. Off, a turn is the whole sequence, so the frames are the same; a refused send is retried from its entry. CoopEngine gains set_replay_pacing and declarations_synced.

Place that differs from upstream's behaviour: TimedEvent is Clone, and the task of the timer runs an event through Arc::get_mut(..).unwrap(), sure that nobody else holds the future. A clone that is alive when the event is due makes the unwrap panic in the task, which ends it, and every event still waiting and every one added later is lost without a word; wz drops that event with an error message and the timer goes on. The timer of wz, like upstream's, can lose an event that was added and then followed at once by a stop, when the event is still in the channel and not in the heap: that is a race of the design and not a difference, and the test avoids it.

One differential file holds the slice, zenoh_util_timer with 9 tests, on the clock: the order events run in (added in no order, added to a timer waiting for a later one, already due), an event that runs once and one defused before and after, the fuse, the handle and the Debug of each, a periodic event that waits one interval before its first run and stops when defused, stop and start in the synchronous and asynchronous forms and with the task spawned blocking, a timer made by each constructor and its clone, the panic outside a runtime, the equality and order of events, the class above, and a control. Round 3657.decision_summary: The bookkeeping of the receive delivery lane exists as a pure value, DeliveryLane, in wz-session-core: the bounded hand-off between the receive path and the task that runs a subscriber's callbacks (docs/rx-delivery-lane.md, phase 2). It bounds a lane by events (a const parameter), bytes and callbacks at once, counts every refusal by reason (saturating), and tells the host where in its own byte area each sample goes. The BYTES stay with the host, a Vec on the heap profile and a static array on the fixed-memory one, so there is one set of rules. Admission is two steps (reserve an event and its bytes, then publish the callbacks it owes), a reserved head holds everything behind it, a sample owing more than the whole budget is admitted only alone, and a wrapped sample is charged the tail it skipped. Nothing reads a limit or a policy yet: the lane takes its bounds as arguments, and the capability, the policy and the three limits land with the tokio host (phase 3).

A full lane refuses the sample and counts it by reason, and the registry's sink has no result channel, so the host counts what was lost apart for samples sent reliably and best-effort through the one function every host asks. There is one lane per offloaded subscription. Round 3677.decision_summary: An offloaded subscriber's full delivery lane can make the session wait for room instead of refusing, and a build or a declaration chooses which: the policy subscriber-overload (block, reject; default block, the blocking handler upstream gives) with SubscribeOptions::with_overload (docs/rx-delivery-lane.md, phase 3b). Under block the sink cannot wait, since it runs under the observer lock the consumer's callback may wait for, so it holds a copy of the sample outside the lane and returns; the drain step the drive loop already awaits admits held samples in order and waits for room, so nothing is lost and a slow callback slows the session. A sample arriving while others are held waits behind them even if the lane has room. A sample longer than the whole byte area could wait for ever, so it is refused under either answer. The lane gains fits and can_ever_fit, which count nothing. The capability rx-callback-offload is not declared: no C ABI door exports the API.

Round 3682.decision_summary: The delivery lane for callbacks off the receive path is measured, on one machine in one condition, against the two deliveries it sits between (docs/rx-delivery-lane.md, phase 6). A burst the lane can hold costs the dispatching loop 35 to 50 us whatever the callback does, where inline it costs n times the callback (12.85 ms for 64 callbacks of 200 us); the lane adds no allocation to the dispatch call, about 0.1 to 0.3 us a sample, and 0 to 1 per cent to the time until the last callback has run. It does not finish the callbacks sooner: there is one consumer. Under block with a burst four times the lane the loop is held for what the lane cannot absorb, as the buffered subscriber's is, and nothing is lost; under reject the loop is never held and 64 of 256 are delivered. Round 3693.decision_summary: A flow's zenoh word is now a sequential probability ratio test, answering the analyzer design's claim that its thresholds belong to wz. Each observation adds a weight in whole millibits, log2 of its likelihood ratio, and the sum is read against +20 and -20 bits (alpha = beta = 2^-20) at every moment, which Ville's inequality bounds for a reader that reads after every packet. Model 1 weighs five checks: cookie_echo and init_roles (handshake), sn_follows judged without the ring when no InitAck gave one (state), version_header (header) and unit_reading (unit). Field widths give the null side of four, the generated corpus the unit one by its largest share, and the zenoh side is assumed until a corpus measures it. A lone Init, Join, Scout or Hello is undecided; a session joined mid-stream is yes on its SN steps. The old word survives as announced_version, and zenoh_evidence carries the sum, the thresholds and each check with its basis.

Round 3695.decision_summary: Phase 3b of the closed key set (docs/closed-key-set.md): a peer's message is delivered by the selection of its key. Round 3704.decision_summary: A peer's reply carrying a key outside a closed key set is now dropped before it reaches a pending query. The reply registry holds a key gate (default: the build's key-set policy, replaceable with set_key_gate) applied at the one seam every reply delivery shares, including the lent and borrowed receive paths. Error replies carry no key and the application's own loopback reply is local, so neither is gated; the peer allowance table is not consulted because a reply answers a query this node asked. Refusals are counted as outside_set and the pending query stays open until its final. Open sets behave as before. Node code still has to pass the same gate to the subscriber table and the reply registry; that adoption is left to the owners of the node images.

Round 3716.decision_summary: The field document moves to revision 45 at the analyzer design's request: each flow's context carries `parameters`, every negotiated value as `{value, basis}` with the basis `stated`, `inferred`, `conflicting` or `absent`, and each half its `lease_ms` the same way. The counts live on the session and not on the context, because the context is kept once per value for every unit and the counts move on every deciding unit. Round 3721.decision_summary: A caller's batching window (zp_batch_start .. zp_batch_stop) is the caller's to drain, as in zenoh-pico, where a frame leaves on an overflow, an express message, a transport message such as a keepalive, or the caller's flush or stop, and never because the writer fell idle (vendor/zenoh-pico/src/transport/common/tx.c). A session on a stream link keeps the link's own window open for good and its writer flushes what is staged when it has nothing to write; that idle flush also drained the caller's window, so each message of a window left as its own frame as soon as the writer was idle. Measured from outside: an external program on the pico C API, linked once to zenoh-pico and once to the wz drop-in, had its peer receive two messages where pico let one through (an express put, then a plain one held in the window), and five where pico let four through (a put that overflowed the batch). The idle flush now stands aside while the caller's window is open.

Round 3754.decision_summary: The policy sn-resolution enters, by the rule of one policy at a time: the width of the sequence numbers the C interfaces advertise, in a unicast InitSyn and in a group's Join. Upstream departed from: zenoh's Resolution default and zenoh-pico's Z_SN_RESOLUTION are 32 bits and there is no setting for another. Choices bits-32 (the default, upstream's), bits-8, bits-16, bits-64. It exists because a peer built with another width refuses wz in a group: pico refuses a Join whose resolution differs from its own (multicast/rx.c), so a wz node was unheard by it. A unicast session already takes the smaller of the two widths, which the negotiation code held. The request-id width is not part of it. The pico ABI on both engines, the zenoh-c ABI and the pico group profile read the one value, SessionPolicy::sn_resolution, so a width is stated once, in the build, with WZ_POLICY_SN_RESOLUTION or its Kconfig symbol.

An unset build run after the stated ones returned to bits-32, so the environment is read at build and not remembered.

Round 3757.decision_summary: Step L2 of the listening role: the cooperative engine holds its links as a table of faces. Core holds a Face (id, link, replay cursor) for each link, the dial role's first at DIAL_FACE (1 << 62, as wz-capi-core keeps it) and never removed, and the registry holds the matching FaceTables (the peer's tables and the session's pending gets). What a declaration, a publish, a plain put, a batch and a keep-alive do reaches every face that is up; a get is one leg for each face and one for the session's own queryables; a write filter and a matching listener count every face's peer, which needed slot_observer's dispatch and link-loss flush to read the other faces (OtherPeers, monomorphic, none for a slot image). A query is answered to the face it came in on: the query plane named the link by the one dialled last, right for one link and wrong for two, so a face now says its generation as its frame is dispatched. Another face comes from CoopEngine::attach_face and goes with its link.

Round 3772.decision_summary: Step L3 of the listening role: the cooperative engine listens. With the feature `listen`, CoopConfig::listen names tcp ports, bound when the engine opens (port 0 allowed, CoopEngine::listening reads them back), and each inbound link becomes a face of its own beside the dial role's, run through the handshake in the acceptor role. The bounds are the config's, at upstream's defaults: accept_pending (100) and max_faces (1000); a connection past either is accepted and closed unread; the handshake's bound is the accepting-inactivity timeout, which is also the face's deadline. An idle read waits on the ports and on every link together (wait_any, one poll on the posix host), not on the first with a bounded look. The acceptor draws its cookie nonce from the session's entropy, so the engine's entropy is shared and CoopEngine::open takes an EntropySource + Send. Off, the engine has no acceptor and no port table. Not done: udp and tls faces, the C ABI's listener.

Round 3806.decision_summary: Step L5 of the listening role: a cooperative session that listens and dials holds one face for each remote zid, as zenoh's transport manager keeps one transport for each. The face table decides when a handshake completes. A second link to a node the session holds is closed with the reason MaxLinks; two links that went the same way keep the first up; two that went opposite ways (two nodes that dialled each other at once) keep the link the lower zid dialled, which both ends compute from the two zids alone, where "the first up" would have each end keep a different link and close both. The dial role's face is never removed, so it stands by (Link::Held) and is dialled again, at once, when the face that held the node is lost; an open of a session that listens and dials is released by the dial's link or by its being held. The rule is the listen feature's: a build that does not listen read 5,000 to 8,000 bytes more with it and cannot reach a node twice.

Round 3810.decision_summary: The link of a cooperative session that listens gives the session nothing between its handshake and the face table's decision. Each link is read through an AdmissionGate: once the session is established and until the engine admits the link, the gate hands the link's task no frame and no end of link, so what the peer sent after the handshake waits in the link, is read in order after the admission, and goes with a link that is refused. This closes the window L5 carried, where a refused link's frames were dispatched in the step that completed its handshake and reached the application once more. A frame in the very batch that completed the handshake is still dispatched and flushed with the lost link. The gate is the listen feature's and wraps only the engine's own links, so the shared session drive and the MCU profiles are unchanged.

Round 3816.decision_summary: The raw Ethernet requirement is held to runs. A reth socket takes CAP_NET_RAW, which no build machine gives a run on its own network, so a raw link's runs are each on a network of their own: bubblewrap puts the run in a new user and network namespace, loopback only, and grants CAP_NET_RAW over that namespace alone with every other capability dropped. Not granting it is how a run is refused raw-ethernet, a refusal by withholding the capability beside the shim's refusals. The shim now brackets the interface ioctls (SIOCGIF*) and can refuse them, so a raw link can be denied the index request it binds by. The build is a registered profile, host-peer-raweth (zenoh-pico's defaults, peer role, raweth transport, unstable API), packaged by Layer C1st and judged on its own runs. The shim's marks no longer overwrite the errno the bracketed call left.

Round 3817.decision_summary: A flake of an older slice, found by round 3815 and carried by it, is explained and mended: a callback of a GET that asks a GET of the queryable that answered it, and waits, failed once in about twenty runs of the same tree. When the drive task took the handler's job, the thread that asked had already finalised and handed the GET's Final to the job's hold; the job released that hold from inside its own call and drained what it staged right there, so the requester's callbacks ran inside the call of the queryable's cell, and the nested GET found the cell mid-call, which parks a call behind the one running. The hold is now released by staging the Final, which the loop that runs the job takes once the job has returned; a hold dropped any other way releases and drains as before. The test has a second thread drain the plane while each ask's final callback asks the same queryable again and waits: it fails without the change (asks 19, 20, 21) and passes with it.

The marks and the repeat were removed and the files restored from the commit before the change.

Round 3822.decision_summary: The 31 KB of text the fixed client carries over single-threaded zenoh-pico was told by owner, and the first lever it ranked is taken: the Keccak permutation of the initial sequence number (2.2 KB, a single symbol that zenoh-pico does not carry). zenoh derives the number from the two zids with SHAKE128 so that a re-attempt of a multilink session lands on the same origin with nothing stored; a client of one link has no use for that, and zenoh-pico draws it from entropy. A feature (initial-sn-compact, CONFIG_WZ_INITIAL_SN_COMPACT) selects a compact pure function of the two zids, FNV-1a over each zid with its length in front and the SplitMix64 finalizer: the same origin for the same pair, a different one at each end and for another peer, a ring of any width. It is not zenoh's value, which a peer cannot tell and a passive dissector that checks a foreign session can, so the default stays the SHAKE128 one and the fixed overlay turns the feature on. The three fixed images fell 2.4 KB of text and their worst chain 428 to 500 bytes; the kit's stack readings did not move, and the images open a session with a real zenohd on the new origin and answer 4,000 queries. Two repairs went with it: the static gates the pre-push hook defers named the new feature, and the scouting tests of the zenoh facade bound a port, read it and released it, which released_port_gate refused; they take free_port now.

Round 3845.decision_summary:
The stack of the fixed-memory client was read for the first time through its calls by register, and the reading found a path the kit never ran. The receive reported every event to one function, the record a frame lends included, so a layer that had a query or a put to send did it from inside that call, on top of the frame the record lies in: in the get image the chain through lend_declare (2,064 bytes) into the sending path (dispatch_network_message_at, 2,456) read 7,640 bytes, over the 6,912 of the 75 percent rule, while the kit's measured peak was 6,112 because no run receives a declaration that is answered by a get. The receive now hands a lent record to its own callee: EventSink has event for the turn's own events and record for a lent record; the dispatch layer answers a record beside it, and the getter and the active layer send what is theirs only on event, after asking the loop to wake (AppWake, raised before the next datagram is read). The two are two slots of one trait object, so a call graph tells them apart. The get image's chain fell to 6,768 bytes, inside the rule; the fixed and batching images read 6,216. Fixed text fell 568 bytes, batching did not move, get grew 72; the get image's kit peak fell 92 bytes to 6,020.

What the 6,216 and 6,768 are, stated as they are: a reading with every call by register given its callees by a rule written for its source line (or its C function), over the functions whose address the image holds (data words, literal pools, movw/movt pairs, adr). It is a bound under those rules and under three assumptions: that a call through a trait object calls the method named on its source line (without it the fixed image reads 7,584), that other threads and interrupts run on their own stacks, and that the recursion of release_cell is as deep as the nesting of slots (two or three). The rules are written by a person and are not yet a gate. This corrects Round 3828 and Round 3842, which read the chain 5,480 to 5,512 as a bound: it follows direct calls only.

Round 3847.decision_summary:
The stack of the fixed-memory images is now held by a bound with the calls through a register followed, and no longer by the worst chain of direct calls and a measurement. scripts/lib/stack_bound_gate.py reads an image built with line tables and, for each call by register in a function the bound reaches, takes the callees from a rule of deploy/stack_call_contracts.json (57 rules) over the functions whose address the image holds; a call no rule claims fails, there is no reading of the vtable slot or of the method named on the line, a rule that says nobody carries its premise (absent, absent_reached) and the gate fails when the premise stops being true, and a cycle is refused unless the contract declares the recursion and its depth. The bound is committed per image (static_bound_bytes: 6,216, 6,216 and 6,768 bytes for the fixed, batching and get images), the quarter of free stack applies to it, and the kit's measured peak must not exceed it, because a measurement above a bound is a hole in the model. The kit lane builds with line tables and runs the step; the three images pass it with their text unchanged (162,216, 166,664 and 174,948).

This corrects two statements of Rounds 3845 and 3846. They said the get image's chain of 7,640 bytes was over the 6,912 of the 75 percent rule. 6,912 is the limit of the fixed image's 9,216-byte stack; the get image's stack is 12,288 bytes, its limit 9,216, and 7,640 was inside it before and after the change of Round 3845. That change was a gain of margin and a removal of a path the kit does not run, not the repair of a rule; its measured effects (the fixed image's text, the get peak, the chain 7,640 to 6,768) stand. The same two rounds called the figure a bound under the rules of a person; it is now a bound under the contract this round commits, which is the same kind of claim with a gate behind it.

The bound still rests on: the rules, written by a person and read against the code; other threads and interrupts on their own stacks; the declared recursion (release_cell three deep, the formatting adapter four); a panic path that ends in an abort. The gate holds those to the image; it does not judge them.

Round 3849.decision_summary:
The main stack of the three fixed images is now a function of the bound the stack bound gate computes, and two holes of that gate are closed. The gate asks each image's overlay for the stack its bound needs, in units of 64 bytes and at most 512 above (a quarter of the stack free): 8,320 for the fixed and batching images (bound 6,216) and 9,024 for the get image (bound 6,768), where they held 9,216, 10,240 and 12,288. RAM fell by exactly that (bss 109,714 to 108,818, 110,786 to 108,866 and 121,482 to 118,218), text did not move, and on the kit the three images boot, answer and read the stack peaks they read before (5,904, 5,908 and 6,020), inside 75 percent of the smaller stacks. A bound that falls now gives the RAM back, and one that rises asks for it, in the same commit.

The second hole: a rule of the contract that names no line (a whole file, a whole C function) claimed every call by register of its file, so a call added there was claimed without anyone reading it. Each such rule now pins, for each image, how many calls it claims (site_pins, 28 rules), and a change of that number fails the gate until the new call is read against the rule's callees. The carry of Round 3847 named this as the rule of exec-poll that could be removed with no gate noticing; the cause was this, and the pin is the repair.

Round 3852.decision_summary: Z6b of the seam note, timestamps, is complete with its query side, and the surface of zenoh falls to 1, 2 and 5 lines of its arms (Query::timestamp_stack goes). Decision: the stack that rides a Push rides the last extension of a Request and of a Response, and the engine carries it as it did for puts while the session records on it. A get gives the options the stack of its loopback leg and that of the Request that leaves; a queryable is shown the stack its query arrived with, which the session completes with its routing and receive; every reply and error reply starts from it and records its send, and the getter is handed the stack of the Response. A Request or Response read in place that carries one takes the owned path. It stays behind the feature pubsub-ts-stack, which unstable selects, so that the client images pay nothing. Carried: a forwarding wz node does not record its route, a lane subscriber has no stack, the receive of a reply is recorded at the callback.

Round 3855.decision_summary:
The dial of the fixed-memory client handed the session's parameters down by value: built in `SlotDialer::dial_expecting`, passed to the host's `dial`, its `open`, `new_session_in_slot` and the slot's `open`. The parameters are 328 bytes (a zid, a 128-byte cookie, a signing key and the queue configuration), and each of those calls kept its own copy in its frame, so the dial's frame held about three of them: 1,224 bytes, the biggest frame of the worst chain after the main loop's. The stack bound gate of Round 3847 made the figure the thing to move, because the main stack is derived from it.

This round hands the slot the function that makes the parameters, not the parameters. `SlotClaim::open`, `new_session_in_slot`, the host's `open` and `dial` (and the lwIP host's `admit` and `dial` over them) take `impl FnOnce() -> SessionInitParams`, and the slot calls it in its own frame, once, where the bundle is built. The slot's `open` is already never inlined, so the copy exists for the length of that call and is gone when it returns. The callers pass `|| factory.borrow_mut().params()` (and `accepted_params()` for an accepted session); the tests that built the parameters first pass `|| params(zid)`.

Measured on the kit lane's three gated images: `dial_expecting` 1,224 to 688 bytes, the slot's `open` 856 to 880 beneath it, the worst chain of direct calls 5,480 to 4,980 (fixed), 5,004 (batching) and 5,224 (get, 5,768 before), and the static bound of the fixed and batching images 6,216 to 6,084. The get image's bound is unchanged, 6,768: its worst path is the lend of a declaration, not the dial. The main stack follows the bound as the gate derives it, 8,320 to 8,128 bytes for the fixed and batching images, 192 less of RAM each. The kit's own peak did not move (5,904, 5,908 and 6,020 in the same rows): the path that sets it is not the dial, so the bytes of stack the firmware uses are as before and only the bytes it reserves fell.

Tried and not kept: building the connect manager's peer entry in place (`PeerEntry::new` written through a pointer into the table's next row, with and without the function never inlined). The entry holds a machine and is about a kilobyte; the compiler did not write the call's result into the row, and the bound read 6,116 and 6,036 against 6,084 without it. The table is as it was. The planner's `open` (1,000 bytes) and `PeerEntry::new` (1,080) are now the worst path of the bound, which is the next place to take frames from.

The rule `answer-reply` of the call contract pins 7 register calls in the answering closure per image, not 6: the inliner emitted one more copy of the closure that calls `keyexpr` and `reply_keyed`, both in the rule's callee set, so the set a site may reach is unchanged. The row of the reason review pins for `session-close-ingress` and `slot_host.rs` is read again: the reason's claim about that file (the host opens sessions in static slots and the lwIP host delegates to it) holds, the parameter type of two methods being all that changed.

Round 3856.decision_summary: The shared-memory watchdog test that failed once on a loaded build host is repaired at its cause, and with it the carry of the last two rounds. conformance/differential/tests/zenoh_shm_metadata.rs had two tests that wait for the periods of the watchdog threads (the confirmator wakes every 50 ms, the validator every 100 ms) with a fixed pause, which a host that keeps a thread from running turns into a failure that is not the crate's. Decision: the run says whether the host kept time, and is made again when it did not. A thread sleeps in steps of 5 ms during the run and keeps its worst lateness; a run on a host whose timers were late by 30 ms or more is made again, up to 8 times, and refused if the host never kept time. A crate that is wrong is wrong in every run: a validator that never invalidates fails both tests in the first one. The repeat is held by a test of its own.

Round 3857.decision_summary:
Round 3855 handed the session's parameters to the slot as a function and cut the dial's frame, and the kit's own reading of the stack did not move. Its verification said so and could not say why. This round finds why: the kit's reading was on another path, the connect manager's planner, which opens a peer for every configured endpoint. There `PeerEntry::new` started its machine in a local (`engine.initialize()`) and moved the local into the entry, so the planner's `open` held the entry (about a kilobyte) and `new` held the local (1,080 bytes) on the same path, with the main loop, `reconcile`, `drive` and `ask` above them: the arithmetic of the bound's worst path then (6,084 bytes) landed within 180 bytes of the kit's reading (5,904).

`PeerEntry::new` now returns the machine as the call's own result, written into the entry as it is returned, and the table starts it once the entry is in its row (`PeerEntry::start`). No unsafe code, no change of row order, the same machine started in the same state. Measured on the kit lane's three images: the kit's reading fell from 5,904 to 5,248 bytes (fixed), 5,908 to 5,248 (batching) and 6,020 to 5,360 (get), 656 bytes on the first two; the static bound of the fixed and batching images 6,084 to 5,972 (get stays 6,768), the main stacks of the first two 8,128 to 8,000 bytes; text +72 bytes. The bound fell less than the reading because its worst path is now another one, the receive's lend of a declaration (`lend_declare`, 2,064 bytes) under a query's answer; the planner's path is below it.

Two things the first attempt of this round got wrong, kept here because the next person will meet the same gate. The first reading of the bound, 5,780, was not a bound: a register call at `query_sink.rs` line 903 was claimed by no rule and the gate does not follow an unclaimed site, so the path through it was missing. The rule for the queryable's function was pinned to line 883 of that file, and another session's commit (Round 3853 and after) moved the call to 903 after the previous round's last kit run; this is a red that was on origin/main after Round 3855 and no hook shows, because the kit lane runs only on the bench host. The rule's line is now 903, the bound reads 5,972, and the pin of `answer-reply` is back to 7 sites (it read 2 while the site was unclaimed because the answering functions it counts in were then not reached at all, the same missing edge).

Round 3860.decision_summary: The receive of a reply to an instrumented get is recorded when the reply arrives, which closes the carried item that recorded it at the callback. Upstream records it at the top of its response handler, ahead of the consolidation, so a Latest query, which holds each reply until the final, received it late in this crate and the timestamp read after the other replies were sent. QueryOptions::with_reply_arrival carries a ReplyArrival, and the ConsolidatingSink calls it on every reply that carries a stack, an error reply and a reply the mode then drops included, and then consolidates the reply as an overlay view that has the completed stack, which is what the Latest cache keeps. wz-zenoh installs the hook for an instrumented get and its reply_of no longer records.

Round 3861.decision_summary: A wz node that forwards a message records its own route on the timestamp stack the message carries, which closes the carried item that left the router and the peer of the mesh out of the stack. Upstream's dispatcher records one ROUTE interception for each face it hands a Push, a Request or a Response to, with the clock of its runtime; here the stamp of the stack was the session's alone and a forwarder passed extension 0x7 through unchanged. Decision: the router hat, which a peer of the mesh is since the linkstate forwarder was folded into it, records at its one egress, egress_to_face, and at the multicast group, which does not pass it, once for each destination; the clock is NodeHlc::interception_timestamp, the node's own or, for a role that stamps no data, a clock of its own over the same source and zid, as upstream's lazy HLC. The bytes are the timestamp of a Put, held to upstream's codec both ways.

Round 3863.decision_summary: The shared-memory arm of the surface of zenoh is closed: Session::get_shm_provider, zenoh::shm::ShmProviderState and OpenBuilder::with_shm_clients, the last three lines the gate held, so the crate states all of upstream's public API in each of its three arms. Decision: the provider of a session is made by the crate from the transport/shared_memory section of the configuration, as upstream's transport manager makes it, and it is not the engine's, which keeps shared memory of its own that shares no type with zenoh::shm. With shared memory off, or its transport optimisation off, there is none; otherwise the pool is made on a thread at the first ask, as upstream's lazy provider is. mode init initialises the subsystem as the session opens. with_shm_clients keeps the storage unread, since the session negotiates no shared memory: an option accepted that does nothing, named. The transport is carried as Z7t with its blocker.

Round 3867.decision_summary:
The matrix of Round 3857 left the fixed image reading 8,548 bytes of stack against 6,060 for the single-threaded zenoh-pico image. The kit's table of threads shows what that is: every thread of the image except the main one is the same in both (the receive thread of the Ethernet driver 1,948 bytes, the net stack's queue 200 to 500, the management thread 248, the system work queue 248, idle 64, the report thread 220 to 300), so the whole gap of 2,488 bytes was the main thread, 5,248 against 2,888. The main thread's frames are the node's own, and the top of the stack there is the main function (1,256), the connect manager's `reconcile` (1,056) and `drive` (800).

`drive` held the planner's actions (six `PeerAction`s, about 300 bytes) as the result of `ask`, again in its own frame, and a third time as the by-value argument of `take`. The actions are one buffer now: `drive` makes it, `ask` pushes to it and `take` reads it in place. `reconcile` put the rows in the list's order by taking the table out of the manager and building it again, two copies of a table in one frame; it rotates each entry's row to the front of the rows not yet placed (a stable reorder, the same order the old code gave, the unnamed rows after in the order they had). The tests of the manager (22, with `adminspace-write`) pass on it.

Round 3878.decision_summary:
The node's loop held its three long-lived parts as locals of one function: the node (448 bytes, of which the connect manager is 352), its factory (68) and the session host (36), with the identity, the plane and the watch beside them. A local of the main function is under every call the loop makes, so the 1,256 bytes of that frame were on the stack of every path of the node, and after Round 3867 they were the biggest frame of the worst chain of direct calls and the biggest piece of what separates the image from the single-threaded zenoh-pico image in the matrix's stack_used (every other thread of the image is equal to pico's; the main thread read 4,280 bytes against 2,888).

The three are built, out of line, in the storage the node already declares as one all-zero `static`: `NodeStorage::run` is a `RunArena`, a bump arena that hands each range out once (`put` builds a value in it from a function, in place, and lends it), the same reason that made the peers' store and the observer cell. `assemble`, never inlined, makes the host, the factory and the node there and returns the node, so what is on its frame while they are built is gone when it returns and the loop holds a reference. `ClientNode` gains the arena's size as a const parameter, and `NodeStorage` the same with a default (`DEFAULT_RUN_BYTES`, 1,024), so an image that states none builds as before. An image states its own and the loop checks it when it is compiled (`run_bytes_needed`, an inline `const` in `assemble`): the Zephyr client says 576 bytes (552 needed), the getter's 704, the secure channel's 1,536, and the secure channel's build is the one that failed the check the first time it was built, with the size its stack type needs. The layer and the acceptor of a node are now bound `'static`, as every image's are.

Measured on the kit's three images: the main function 1,256 to 704 bytes (the getter's 1,368 to 816), the direct chain 4,172 to 3,620 (4,756 to 4,204), the static bound 5,972 to 5,420 (6,768 to 6,216), the kit's reading 4,280 to 3,728 (5,104 to 4,552), the main stacks to 7,232, 7,232 and 8,320 (they were 8,000, 8,000 and 9,024); `.bss` +576 bytes, text +244 (161,588, 166,044 and 174,212, inside the rows' tolerance). The secure channel's image, which has no row, reads a bound of 6,224 against 7,592.

One rule of the call contract is pinned to a line of `slot_node.rs`, the factory's call of the entropy function, and the code added above it moved the line from 678 to 774; the unclaimed site was the gate's first sentence on the new build, and the rule is moved.

Round 3885.decision_summary: The message counter of a receive path that runs on several threads is a lock-free IntervalMeter, and the snapshot's interval statistic is now buckets plus the sum of the intervals instead of buckets plus an exponentially weighted mean. The sum gives the exact mean of any window from two snapshots, costs a fetch-add where the weighted mean cost a compare-and-swap loop, and every count is 64 bits and cumulative, so none saturates (a 32-bit bucket froze after 71 minutes at a million messages a second). A receiver reads the clock and then stores, so its reading can be a little behind the latest; counting that as an interval put two spans in the histogram that no gap made, one backwards and the next inflated by the receiver's delay. The rule is now that such a message is counted and makes no interval, a span of half the clock's range or more is no interval and moves the latest, and the single-thread MessageStats takes the same rule. The layout version 1 changes (header 64 bytes, 8 per bucket) because no reader exists yet.

Round 3886.decision_summary:
After Round 3878 the deepest path of the fixed-memory client's stack was the handshake's parse: the main function under the executor, the unit's dispatch, its decode, and `parse_init`, whose frame was 1,008 bytes. The cause was the same as in the rounds before it, found by the same measure: a transport message (an `InboundFrame`, 712 bytes on the fixed profile, its extension chain being 520 of them) was handed on by value. `parse_init` built it in a local and wrapped it in a `Result` that its caller held a slot for; the decode of the unit and the judgement of it took the result as a value.

The decode now writes the message into a slot its caller lends. `parse_unit_into` is the decoder, with the same arms and the same errors; it returns where the message ended. The handshake arms (`parse_init`, `parse_open`, `parse_close`) and the keep-alive build the message in the slot and read its extension chain where it lies, which is what the codec's own `decode_into` does for the chain. The decoders the profiles with a heap and the tests call (`parse_inbound`, `parse_inbound_consuming` and the shared-unit one) keep their signatures and are the same decode over a local slot. `SessionLinkActions` gains `handle_inbound_consuming_into` and its shared-unit twin, which also record what the link learns of the message. The unit's dispatch (`dispatch_unit_in`) owns the one slot, `decode_unit_in` writes it and `decide_unit_in` reads it, by reference; the heap profile's `Frame` and `Fragment` still move their payload out of it into the outcome (`take_decoded`), and the profile with no heap is lent the slot.

Measured on the kit's three images: the handshake's parse is no longer the worst chain. The worst is the dial now (`reconcile`, `drive`, `dial_peer`, `dial_expecting` and the slot's `open`, 3,564 bytes over 7 frames, against the parse's 3,620 over 13), so the gain shows as far as the dial lets it: the kit's reading fell 88 bytes to 3,640 (fixed) and 64 to 3,664 (batching); the get image's worst chain is not this one and did not move. The bound stays 5,420 and 6,216, set by the receive's lend of a declaration. The text moved by under the tolerance.

One experiment that did not hold, kept so it is not tried again: `parse_init` returning its own `Result` built as one local with one return, with a chain error recorded into it and not returned from the middle, read 3,628 against 3,620. The compiler keeps its own copy of a value built in a local and returned; only a slot the caller lends removes it.

Round 3890.decision_summary: A callback of the top crate no longer runs on the thread that reads a face. That thread drives a single-threaded runtime, so a callback that waits on another thread (upstream's tests do, with block_in_place) was refused or never returned. What a face hands an entity is queued in the order it came, and one task of the receive runtime at a time calls the callback; a caller that may block calls it where it stands. A liveliness get counts in the session's callback group, so a close that waits for callbacks waits for it. A get also consolidates across its legs: each leg consolidated its own face, so two peers answering a key gave two replies where upstream gives one. A malformed access control is refused in upstream's words, in its order. The upstream files callback_drop_on_undeclare, cancellation, unicity and the access control config test pass.

Round 3893.decision_summary: A C program takes and reads the node's resource snapshot through four doors, wz_ext_snapshot_set_source, _poll, _size and _read, under the resource-snapshot capability. The program's source is called with no lock of the library held, so Sampler::poll is split into is_due and take: the door asks is_due under the lock, calls the source outside it, and takes under the lock again. The node's received-message count is the engine's to answer (SessionEngine::message_reading, none by default) and the core engine sums its faces' counters; the counters of a face that has gone are added to a retained total in the same step that removes the face, so the node's count never falls when a link does and a reader may take windows by subtraction. A joined group's members are not counted: their receive path feeds no meter. The host source, the features word and the readers are the next step.

Round 3894.decision_summary:
After Round 3889 the fixed-memory client's first tick, which dials, read 3,208 bytes of stack, and the slot's `open` with what it calls (`ext_chain_of`) were 1,068 bytes of the dial's chain. The frame of `open` held the session's bundle as a value of that function and, inside it, four handshake ext chains of 200 bytes each (two Init chains with the patch entry, two empty Open chains), each made as a value and copied into its field.

The bundle is now written in its slot field by field. `SessionLinkActions::build_in` writes the link half and the kernel half into the slot's storage through `write_fields!`, which takes the same `name: expr` list a struct literal takes, writes each field in a block of its own, and destructures the list without `..` in a closure that is never called, so a field left out of the list does not compile as it would not in a literal. The heap profiles keep `build`, which uses the same two functions over locals and wraps the halves in the runtime's shared pointer, so the list is written once. The four chains are each written by `init_ext_chain`, a function of its own and never inlined: two values made in one function were two slots of its frame however the statements were cut, which the first attempt (one function, each field in a block) showed: the frame of `init_core` was 720 bytes and the chain grew to 3,516. `ExtChainBuf::one` and `ext_chain_of` are gone, the chain being built in the place it is kept.

Measured on the kit's three images: the dial's frames under `wz_app_main` fell from 1,068 to about 570 bytes (`open` 520, `init_core` 32, the chain writer 16), and the first tick reads 3,048. The worst chain of direct calls is now the handshake's parse (the receive of an Init: the executor, `dispatch_unit_borrowed` 768 with the 720-byte inbound frame, `decode_unit_in` 320, `parse_init` 432, `decode_handshake_ext_chain_into` 304), 3,088 bytes over 13 frames, and it sets the kit's reading at 3,192 (3,208 before). The bound stays 4,240. The text moved by 32 bytes.

Two experiments that did not hold, kept so they are not tried again: the four chains as an empty constant given their entry after the bundle is placed (each `new_mutex(CONST)` was still a 204-byte slot, and `open` grew from 856 to 1,080), and the loop's log lines said by one out-of-line function (the frame of `wz_app_main` stayed 704 bytes and the text grew 232).

Round 3896.decision_summary:
After Round 3894 the handshake's parse was the longest chain of direct calls of the fixed-memory client (3,088 bytes over 13 frames) and set the kit's reading at 3,192. Its largest frame was `dispatch_unit_borrowed`, 768 bytes, which holds the inbound frame the decoder is lent: 720 bytes, of which the extension chain was 520. The four messages that carry a chain (Init, Open, Close, KeepAlive) held it as an array of eight owned entries of 65 bytes, the decoder's own bound, and read every entry of the chain into it.

A received handshake chain on `session-slot` is now `ReceivedExtChain`: the header byte of every entry (eight bytes, in the chain's order) and the entries only of the extensions this build reads. Which those are is `reads_received_ext`: the patch level and the remote bound (one id, on the Init and the Open), the region name, and one for each feature that compiles a reader (quality of service, low latency, compression, shared memory, authentication, multilink); the number kept is bounded by `RECEIVED_EXT_KINDS`, three in the smallest build. The admission rule (`judge_ext_chain`) takes the headers and nothing else, so it sees the same bytes in the same order and judges a message as before, an unknown mandatory extension being refused by its header whether the entry was kept or not; the readers look an extension up by its id and by its identity in what is kept. The chain is judged through a trait (`ChainHeaders`, crate-private) that the heap profile's `Vec` and the slice also implement. The decoder refuses a chain past the bound of eight entries as before, and a peer that repeats an extension the build reads until the kept entries are full, as a chain past the bound.

Measured on the kit's three images: the worst chain of direct calls fell from 3,088 to 3,024 bytes and is the dial's again (the session pump's `build_in`, the engine's microsteps, `send_open_syn`); the handshake's parse is below it. The kit's reading fell from 3,192 to 3,048 bytes (the first tick's) in 1 of 1 run on the fixed and the batching image, the get image holds its row, the bound stays 4,240, 4,240 and 5,036. The text grew by 104 bytes (160,724 to 160,828).

The ext identity gate classifies the one site that reads the 4-bit id here as a hint: it decides what is kept, a look-alike of the same id is kept too, and no reader takes an entry for its extension by the id.

Round 3899.decision_summary:

The actions are a field of the manager (`ConnectManager::actions`): the manager lives in the node's storage, and `drive` is on the stack of the thread that ticks it. `ask` pushes into the field, `take` reads one action at a time by index (the arms borrow the manager whole), and `drive` clears it before each call; `drive` is not its own callee and nothing `take` calls enters it, so the field is empty between two calls. The node grew by the buffer and the loop's compile-time check of the run arena refused the first build, which is what it is there for; the arena (`RUN`) is 256 bytes larger on the three images. A new row is built in the table's row: `BoundedVec::push_with` takes the function that makes the value and, on a fixed table, writes it into the slot (on a growable one it is `push` of the result), and says whether there was room.

Round 3901.decision_summary: The four instruments of the observation plane are linked through the C doors. A supervised checkpoint that misses its deadline writes one event into the node's log before the program's hook runs, so the expiry is in the log whatever the hook does. Round 3905.decision_summary:
After Round 3900 the bottom of the fixed-memory client's stack was one frame of 704 bytes that every chain of calls stood on: the entry function, `wz_app_main`, which had inlined `fixed_client::run` and `ClientNode::run`. The set-up of the node (the 152-byte `ClientNode` value, the identity, the signing key, the stack, the factory's parts, the zid in two forms) and the loop that goes round for the life of the node were one function's slots, so the frame was as large as the set-up needed and stayed that large under the loop.

`ClientNode::run` is now `start` and a loop. `ClientNode::start` does everything `run` did before its first round and returns `RunningNode`: the tasks' pool, the node by reference (it lives in the storage's arena), the plane, the application, the clock and the watch, a few words. `RunningNode::drive`, the loop, is `NodeLoop::drive`, a trait so that a platform's function can return the node as `impl NodeLoop` without spelling its types. `run` is the two in sequence, which is what the Linux host node calls; an application held by reference is an application (`impl NodeApp for &mut A`) so that it keeps lending its own. The Zephyr image's `fixed_client::run` holds the console and what `start` hands back; its set-up is its own function, `start`, out of line, with `ClientNode::start` inlined into it, and its frame is gone before the first round.

Measured on the kit's three images: the entry function is 176 bytes of frame and the loop 400, where the one function was 704. The worst chain of direct calls fell from 2,784 to 2,616 bytes (fixed and batching) and from 4,008 to 3,388 (get); the dial is the longest chain again. The stack bound fell from 3,816 to 3,352, from 4,016 to 3,488 and from 4,744 to 4,580, and the main stacks that follow it from 5,120 to 4,480, from 5,376 to 4,672 and from 6,336 to 6,144 bytes. The kit's reading fell from 2,888 to 2,696 bytes on the fixed and the batching image and from 4,552 to 4,328 on the get image, in 1 run each. The text fell by 424, 472 and 664 bytes (160,356, 164,732 and 172,724): the symbol table shows `check_outbound_keyexpr_pico_safe`, `TimerQueue::pop_expired` and `run_until_idle` (946 bytes) standing on their own before and inlined into the loop now; why the compiler inlines them into the loop and did not into the old entry function was not looked at. The owners of the text moved with it: the 3,594 bytes of the old entry function were counted as `c:wz_` (the owner of a symbol is read off its name, and the entry function's is a C name) and are `wz_session_mcu` and `wz_zephyr_admin_node` now. Two rules of the stack call contracts moved their pins: `planner-call` from 1 to 3 sites (`ask` is inlined at more places; the callees it is held to are the same) and `app-main` from 2 to 0 (the entry function holds no trait-object call any more).

What the matrix of Round 3900 showed about the cell that is lost, `stack_used` (6,188 bytes of wz against 6,060 of the single-thread pico image), is recorded here because it decides which work counts. The kit's threads other than the main one are the same in both images to the byte, except the network stack's receive thread (`rx_q`), which read 496 bytes in 3 of wz's 12 boots and 368 in all of pico's. The captures of the 24 boots say why: in exactly those 3 wz boots the router sent 4 datagrams (1, 1, 50 and 50 bytes) to a port that the previous boot's session had held, and in the 12 pico boots it sent none. The lane flashes an image, which boots and dials, and resets it; wz has dialled by then and pico has not, so the router holds a session of a boot that is gone, and the network stack answers a datagram for a closed port in the receive thread, which is a deeper path than a delivery. This is a property of the lane's sequence and of wz dialling faster; the lane was not changed for it.

Three experiments that did not hold, kept so they are not tried again: `ClientNode::start` as a call of its own (161,700 bytes of text, 920 more than the image before for the same frames: the node was passed by value across the call and each function paid a prologue); the loop's log lines said by one out-of-line function, tried in the loop (the loop stayed 392 bytes, its slots being the tick's inlined, and the text grew 136) and before that in the entry function (it stayed 704, the text grew 232); and the four handshake ext chains as an empty constant (each `new_mutex(CONST)` was still a 204-byte slot).

Both hosts are asked for it by a wz session in Layer E7g and E6f, which also holds that a router's count survives the link that carried it. Round 3908.decision_summary:
After Round 3905 the fixed-memory client that only answers was 160,356 bytes of text, 15 KB over the single-thread zenoh-pico image it is compared with, and the symbol table has no large single piece: the largest wz functions are 1 to 3 KB. One family of them is the receive's decoders. The slot profile reads each record of a frame where it lies, one decoder for each kind of message (`lend_push`, `lend_request`, `lend_response`, `lend_declare`, `lend_response_final`, `lend_interest`, `lend_oam`, 6.4 KB with what they inline), and this client carried all of them. It declares no subscriber (the pico it is compared with has `Z_FEATURE_SUBSCRIPTION` off) and asks no query, so no router sends it a Push, a Response or a ResponseFinal; only the Request it is there for. Turning the three arms into the unknown MID for a measurement took the text to 155,300 bytes, 5,056 less.

A node reads a kind off the wire only if it asked for it, and says so in its features. `wz-session-core` has two selectors, `rx-push` and `rx-response`, which pull no codec (the codec of a kind writes it too: a queryable writes Responses and a publisher Pushes). A capability that makes a node read a kind turns the selector on: `declare-subscriber` and `adminspace-write` (a config write is a Put on an admin key) for the Push; `query-get`, in the core and in `wz-session-mcu`, for the Response and the ResponseFinal; `session-unicast-accept` and `session-multicast` for both, because a node a peer opens a session to, or a group member, is written to and asked. The decoders, the helpers that judge them, the arms of the slot walk, the variants of `WalkedRecord` and `LentRecord`, the constructors and the sink arms are compiled under the selector on the slot profile and, as before, whenever there is a heap; `InPlaceRecord::push`, `response` and `response_final` keep their signatures and answer `None` where the kind is not read. A frame that carries a kind the build did not ask for ends its walk at that record, as a MID with no decoder ends it; a router does not send one.

Measured on the kit's three images: the text of the answering client fell from 160,356 to 153,868 bytes (6,488 less, `wz_session_core` 4,044 and `wz_codecs` 2,386 of them) and its bss by 640; the batching image fell 6,480 to 158,252 and its stack bound from 3,488 to 3,352, the same as the fixed one's (its overlay stack 4,672 to 4,480); the get image, which reads the Responses of its own queries, fell 1,688 to 171,036. Two rules of the stack call contracts moved their pins with the sites that went: `record` from 6 to 3 (5 on the get image) and `own-mapping` from 2 to 1. The answering images answered 2,000 queries of each document, and the get image's getter said how its queries went.

The kit lane caught a mistake of the first version of this change, which is why it is recorded: `wz-session-mcu`'s `query-get` turned on the codecs of the Response and not the selector, so the get image never read a Response and the lane said "no getter line after the reset in 150 s". `query-get` turns `rx-response` on in the mcu crate now.

Round 3910.decision_summary: A router session hosts a queryable, carries a delete, and declares a publisher and a querier whose matching it reads from its tables. A queryable the router hosts is a branch of the fan of a query: it answers from its handler, or keeps the query and answers later, and the final goes when the last hold is dropped. A matching status or listener of a router counts the declarations of its links by locality (the node's own are the session's, the faces' are remote), and the node's face is told each time the tables are written. Two faults the upstream matching file showed are fixed: a peer retracts by id alone, which the mesh hat of the peer region could not resolve, so the router keeps the key each face declared under each id; and a reply for a resource was folded and kept backed by every queryable that intersects it, where zenoh takes the resource's own, so a querier that wants complete queryables kept a completeness that was gone. The upstream matching file passes (24 of 24).

Round 3911.decision_summary:
Round 3908 made a node read a Push or a Response off the wire only if it asked for it. The slot profile's walk had three more decoders the answering client did not use: the Declare, the Interest and the Oam of a peer (`lend_declare`, `lend_interest`, `lend_oam`, 2.2 KB with what they inline). Their consumers on that client are the registries of remote declarations, whose limits the kit's configuration keeps at zero (`MAX_REMOTE_DECLS`, `MAX_INBOUND_SUB_INTERESTS`), the token registry that answers an interest (the client holds no token) and nothing for the Oam, which the walk only judges. The client sends no Interest, and the pinned router declares a key expression to a face only when the face is on its north side or sent a key-expression interest (`zenoh/src/net/routing/dispatcher/resource.rs` @ `pub fn decl_key`) and a subscriber only to a face with a matching interest (`zenoh/src/net/routing/hat/broker/pubsub.rs` @ `.filter(|(_, i)| i.options.subscribers() && i.matches(res))`), which was read in the pinned source and not assumed.

`wz-session-core` has a third selector, `rx-control`, that pulls no codec, turned on by what makes a node use the control records of a peer: `declare-subscriber`, `declare-token`, `liveliness-token`, `liveliness-subscriber`, `liveliness-get`, `session-unicast-accept` and `session-multicast`. `query-get` does not turn it on: a client that asks is answered and told nothing it did not ask. The decoders, the verdict functions they share, the arms of the slot walk, the variants of `WalkedRecord` and `LentRecord`, the constructors and the sink arms are compiled under it; `InPlaceRecord::declare` and `interest` keep their signatures and answer `None` without it. A shared verdict function (`judge_chain`) is compiled on the union of its callers, as the comment above it says every item of that file is; a slot build that reads no kind of record at all (`wz-runtime-coop --features session-slot`, which compiled before) needed the two enums to hold their lifetime in a variant that is never made and four items to say they may be unused.

Measured on the kit's three images: the text of the answering client fell from 153,868 to 148,948 bytes (4,920 less, `wz_session_core` 3,488 and `wz_codecs` 1,354 of them); the batching image fell 5,016 to 153,236 and the get image 4,488 to 166,548. Since Round 3905 the fixed image has lost 11,408 bytes of text (160,356 to 148,948). The stack bound, chain and readings did not move. The contracts lost the sites of the Declare and the Interest: `record` from 3 to 1 (3 on the get image) and `own-mapping` from 1 to 0 (it stays 1 on the get image). The fixed and the batching image answered 2,000 queries of each document and the get image's getter said how its queries went, as before.

An experiment before the change, with the three arms taken out of the walk and the rest left linked, measured 3,560 bytes: the change is 1,360 more, because the verdict function the three share and the sink arms were then unused too. In that experiment the fixed image's stack reading read 2,728, outside its row of 2,696; in the change it reads inside the row. Why the experiment read 32 bytes more was not looked at.

Round 3915.decision_summary:
After Round 3911 the answering client's symbol table named one floating-point expression: the growth of the retry wait in `RetryPeriod::next_ms`, `(delay_ms as f64 * factor) as u64`, which is upstream's (`connection_retry.rs`: `(self.delay as f64 * factor) as i64`). On a target with no double-precision unit it is a call to the compiler's soft-float multiply, two conversions and two comparisons: `__muldf3` 778 bytes, `__aeabi_d2ulz` 116, `__aeabi_ul2d` 112, `__aeabi_dcmpge` 114, `__aeabi_dcmpgt` 106 and `__aeabi_dmul` 12, 1,238 bytes, all called from the planner's `perform` and from nothing else.

`retry_period::grown_ms` returns the expression's value for every input and does no floating-point operation. It does what the expression does and in the same order: the delay rounded to the nearest `f64` (exact below 2^53), multiplied by the factor's mantissa as an integer, the exact product rounded to 53 significant bits (nearest, ties to even), then truncated and saturated as `as u64` does; an infinite, NaN, negative, zero or subnormal factor and a delay of 0 are resolved by the rules of IEEE 754 and `as`. `RetryPolicy` keeps its `f64` field, which is upstream's type, the config's and 20 crates' to name; the schedule is one implementation for every profile, so the host and the board cannot differ in it. Two tests hold it equal to the expression: over a grid of the edges (delays around 2^53 and 2^64; factors exact, inexact, tiny, huge, subnormal, infinite, NaN and negative) and over 250,000 random pairs of bit patterns, delay and factor, plus factors near 1 and small multiples of 1/1024, which are the ones whose product rounds across an integer (1.7 times 10 is 16.999999999999999556 exactly and 17 as an `f64`, where an exact floor would say 16).

Measured on the kit's three images: the soft-float routines are no longer in the image; `round_to_significant` is 372 bytes and the arithmetic inlined at the manager's two calls the rest of 558, so the text fell 680 bytes (148,948 to 148,268) on the fixed image and 672 on the batching (152,564) and the get image (165,876). The stack chain, bound and readings did not move. The rows of the text budget moved by less than their tolerance and were not moved. Taking `grown_ms` out of line, one copy for the two calls, was 40 bytes more (148,308) and was not kept.

Round 3920.decision_summary:
After Round 3915 the symbol table of the answering client named `wz_session_mcu::dial::parse_locator` at 886 bytes, the one function the slot dialer calls at two places to read `udp/<a.b.c.d>:<port>`. It was written with `str::strip_prefix`, a search for either of two characters, `rsplit_once`, `split('.')` and the generic `str::parse::<T>`, which the compiler writes once for each integer width (the u8 of an octet, the u16 of the port).

`dial::decimal` now reads the digits of both numbers against a maximum, one function for both widths, and the endpoint is scanned as bytes. The function is 386 bytes: the text fell 496 bytes on the fixed image (148,268 to 147,772) and on the batching (152,564 to 152,060) and the get image (165,876 to 165,372). What the parser accepts and refuses is the same set: the tests of the refusals are kept (a `+` sign, a port of 0, 256, a fifth field, a name, a bracketed address, `?` and `#`) and eleven cases are added for what the generic reader decided silently: empty fields in each place, a number wider than any integer, leading zeros, and the widest port and octets.

The same build found two things that were already red and are repaired here. The line-pinned rule `entropy-draw` of `deploy/stack_call_contracts.json` named `session_actions.rs:6150`; a commit of another session (`c2bc91eb85`) moved the call to 6148, and the stack bound of every gated image refused it ("calls through a register at session_actions.rs:6148 and no rule claims the site"). No hook runs the kit lane, so the push of that commit did not see it; the pin is now 6148. And the text rows of the three images are moved to the figures the images read, 147,772, 152,060 and 165,372: Round 3915's 680 bytes were within the tolerance and are now 1,176 together with this change, over it.

Round 3921.decision_summary: A buffer of shared memory crosses the engine in both directions between sessions of the top crate. The process holds two shared-memory systems (zenoh::shm and the engine's) that agree on the protocol and share no type, so the buffer is carried and not converted. The engine publishes any chunk a host owns (ShmPublishable) and reads a received descriptor with a resolver the host supplies (ShmReader::Host). The top crate wraps the slice of a ZBytes as the send buffer, takes the receiver's reference as upstream's codec does, reads a descriptor with its own reader into a ZShm, and offers shared memory at the handshake. A put at or over message_size_threshold is copied into the session's provider when some peer shares memory; a subscriber of the session keeps the bytes. The upstream shm file passes 8 of 10 (from 1); the two multicast tests need a group that carries descriptors.

Round 3922.decision_summary: A multicast group whose transports are shared-memory ones carries descriptors. Upstream gives a multicast transport a shared-memory context when the session holds one, maps every message it sends to its partner whatever the protocol, and reads every message it receives, with no handoff because the group is unreliable. The engine now does the same per group: Session::enable_shm stamps the group's registries as reading shared memory once, when its session is made (a group negotiates nothing a reconnect could lower), the node's reader is installed on it, and publish_shm_on_group puts ONE descriptor on the wire for every member. The fan-out sends a chunk to such a group as its descriptor and any other group the bytes; has_shm_peer counts these groups, so a large put is promoted for a session whose only peers are a group. The top crate reports its groups as shared-memory ones. The upstream shm file passes 10 of 10.
